## Lab Reports

Brief reports explain the questions, methods, findings, and limitations of recent lab publications.

::: {.card}
<p class="chip">Zenodo · 2026</p>
### [Causal Questions Before Statistical Models](reports/nzavs-lmtp-workflow.qmd)
Version 1 of the lab's registered workflow for longitudinal causal studies in the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study. We register all our code and hypotheses in advance of estimation. This improves on the traditional "verbal" approach, which leaves many researcher degrees of freedom. The code is our registration, and any deviations are recorded as diffs in the code.
:::

::: {.card}
<p class="chip">PLOS One · 2026</p>
### [Work Hours, Fatigue, and Physical Health](reports/work-hours-wellbeing.qmd)
A target trial emulation among 24,579 pre-retirement New Zealanders estimates what happens when weekly work hours shift up or down by ten. On average, working ten extra hours increases fatigue, with smaller, more fragile effects on sleep, body mass index, and perceived physical health.
:::

::: {.card}
<p class="chip">Evolutionary Human Sciences · 2026</p>
### [Religious Attendance and Selective Gains in Well-being](reports/religious-attendance-wellbeing.qmd)
A target trial emulation examines an intervention that makes monthly religious service attendance more probable among baseline non-attenders. We find small causal effects on meaning and purpose, forgiveness, and (surprisingly) sexual satisfaction. In one way or another, we suspect these outcomes all have to do with coordination. Estimates for psychological distress (anxiety, depression, rumination) and most physical-health outcomes (sleep, fatigue, alcohol use) are near zero. Many cross-sectional associations reported in the literature appear to reflect confounding rather than a causal effect of starting to attend.
:::
